newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court upholds Commission right to protect against pig fever.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds Commission right to protect against pig fever.

text.p: The European Court of First Instance dismissed on Tuesday an action for damages brought by German farmers against the European Commission.

The farmers claimed the Commission overreached its authority when it banned the sale of pigs not only from Germany to other member states, but also between states within Germany, to control swine fever.
The Commission's decisions prohibited the sale of pigs from the applicant's farm because of the location of the farm, even though no incidence of swine fever had occurred there.

Council directive 90/425 governing veterinary checks on pigs sold between member states allows for preventive measures to contain swine fever. The Commission took further decisions to stop the export of pigs on a region by region basis.

The applicants argued the court should characterise the Commission's decisions as administrative, rather than legislative, and apply the less stringent standard of "unlawful act" to determine liability.
The court rejected their arguments, finding the Commission did not discriminate against the applicants nor take decisions that were inappropriate or disproportionate.
Aloys Schroder, Jan Thamann and Karl-Julius Thamann, applicants
Commission of the European Communities, defendant

application for an award of damages under article 178 and the second paragraph of article 215 of the EC treaty against the Commission for damage allegedly suffered by the aplicants as a result of a series of decisions adopted by the Commission to control classical swine fever in the Federal Republic of Germany
2. Orders the applicants to pay the costs.
